name: Printing Table of Medal Counts with Row Totals
description:
Assume that we have a 7x4 matrix that stores the number of medals that seven countries won in the skating competitions at the Winter Olympic. This matrix looks like as follows:
[[ "Canada", 1, 0, 1 ],
 [ "China", 1, 1, 0 ],
 ...]
Each row of this matrix corresponds to the medal counts for the country in that row. The second, third, and fourth numbers within a row represent the number of Gold, Silver, and Bronze medals won by the corresponding country in that row.
Construct a program that takes this matrix and prints a table of medal counts with row total that shows the number of Gold, Silver, Bronze, and Total medals for each of the countries who participated in the competition. The output table should look like as follows:
    Country    Gold  Silver  Bronze   Total
     Canada        1       0       1            2
        China        1       1       0            2
       ...
code:
#Step 1: Define a 7x4 matrix that stores the number of medals won by seven countries
medal_counts = [[ "CAN", 1, 0, 1 ],
                [ "CHN", 1, 1, 0 ],
                [ "GER", 0, 0, 1 ],
                [ "KOR", 1, 0, 0 ],
                [ "JPN", 0, 1, 1 ],
                [ "RUS", 0, 1, 1 ],
                [ "USA", 1, 1, 0 ]]
#Step 2: Print the header of the output table
print("{:>4s}{:>3s}{:>3s}{:>3s}{:>4s}".format("Name","G","S","B","All"))
#Step 3: Iterate through the rows in the medal counts matrix
for i in range(len(medal_counts)):
    #Step 3.1: Assign initial values to variables we need for printing row i
    line = "{:>4s}".format(medal_counts[i][0])
    row_total = 0
    #Step 3.2: Iterate through the columns that have medal counts
    for j in range(1, len(medal_counts[0])):
        #Step 3.2.1: Append medal counts to the content of row i
        line += "{:>3d}".format(medal_counts[i][j])
        #Step 3.2.2: Update the row total for row i 
        row_total += medal_counts[i][j]
    #Step 3.3: Add the row total to the content of the output table for row i
    line += "{:>3d}".format(row_total)
    #Step 3.4: Print the content of the output table for row i
    print(line)

commentList: This line assigns a list (the outer list) to the variable medal_counts and starts the first inner list row: ["CAN", 1, 0, 1]. That inner list encodes one country's data: index 0 is the country code "CAN", index 1 is Gold, index 2 is Silver, and index 3 is Bronze.

Syntax-wise this is a list literal containing another list. The inner list mixes a string ("CAN") and three integers (1, 0, 1). The trailing comma and newline show that more rows follow on the next lines — Python allows a list to span multiple lines.

Be careful about types: later the code uses string formatting that expects a str for the name ("{:>4s}") and ints for medals ("{:>3d}"). If you accidentally put the numbers in quotes (e.g. "1") or the name as a non-string, you can get TypeError during formatting.

Common syntax errors you might hit here: forgetting the comma after this inner list, mismatching or missing quotes around "CAN", or not closing the outer list with ] at the end — all of those cause a SyntaxError.

Best practices you can follow: keep each row the same length (4 elements) so indexing is consistent, use clear country names or consistent codes, and consider validating rows before printing. For clearer code in larger programs, you could use a dict or a small object instead of mixed-type lists.

commentList: Purpose: This line prints the header row for your output table so you (and anyone reading the program) can see the column labels: Name, G, S, B, and All. It creates the top line that aligns with the numeric rows printed later.

How it works (syntax and semantics): print(...) writes text to the screen. Inside, a format string with five fields "{:>4s}{:>3s}{:>3s}{:>3s}{:>4s}" tells Python to take the five arguments given to .format(...) and place each into a fixed-width slot. For each slot, > means right-align and the number (4, 3, 3, 3, 4) is the minimum field width; the trailing s says you expect a string. The .format("Name","G","S","B","All") supplies the five header labels in order to those slots.

Common errors and misconceptions to watch for: if you pass a non-string where a {:s} is used (for example an int), Python will raise a TypeError; make sure the number of items in .format(...) matches the number of fields or you'll get an IndexError; the widths are minimums — if a label or data item is longer than the width it will expand the column, not truncate it; and > means right-align (not center or left). Also note there are no extra spaces between the fields in the format string, so you control spacing only via the widths you choose.

Best practices and tips: choose widths that match your longest expected country name and your largest numbers so columns stay aligned (e.g., use a larger width for the name). If you want clearer spacing, add explicit spaces in the format string (for example "{:>10s} {:>4s}...") or increase the numeric widths. For readability in your code you can also use f-strings or a small helper function to build rows, but the .format approach shown here is fine for simple tables.

commentList: Purpose: This line starts a loop that visits each row of the medal_counts matrix so you can build and print one output line per country. It ensures the program processes all seven country rows (or however many rows exist).

Syntax and semantics: for introduces a loop; range(len(medal_counts)) produces the sequence 0, 1, ..., n-1 where n is the number of rows; i is the loop variable that will take each index; the trailing colon (:) begins the indented block that runs for each i. Inside the block you use medal_counts[i] to access the i-th row.

How it contributes: By giving you the row index i, this line lets you access the country name and its medal counts with medal_counts[i][0], medal_counts[i][1], etc., which you then format and print to produce the table row-by-row.

Common mistakes to watch for: If medal_counts is empty, the loop body won't run — that is normal but you might want to handle that case. Be careful with off-by-one thinking: range(len(...)) goes from 0 up to len-1. Also avoid modifying the medal_counts list (adding/removing rows) while iterating, because that can cause unexpected behavior.

Assumptions and pitfalls related to other code: This loop assumes each row has the same number of columns because later code uses len(medal_counts[0]) for the inner loop. If rows differ in length you can get index errors when accessing medal_counts[i][j].

Best practices: You can make this clearer and safer by using a more descriptive name (for example for row_idx in range(len(medal_counts)):), or by iterating directly over rows (for row in medal_counts:) when you don't need the index. If you do need both index and row, use enumerate(medal_counts).

commentList: Purpose: you set row_total = 0 to give yourself a starting value for adding up the medals for the current country; this variable will hold the running total for that row.
Syntax/semantics: this is a simple assignment that binds the integer 0 to the name row_total. Because this line runs inside the outer loop, you reset the total for each new country.

Potential errors and misconceptions: if you forget to reset row_total here (for example by placing the initialization outside the loop), totals will accumulate across rows and give wrong results. Also, if you initialize it to a non-integer (like None or a string), you'll get a TypeError when you try to add numbers to it.

Best practices: initialize the accumulator immediately before the inner loop so it's clear you're starting a fresh total for this row. Use a descriptive name like row_total (as shown). As an alternative, you could compute the sum in one step with sum(medal_counts[i][1:]) for clarity, but the explicit loop with row_total = 0 is fine for learning how accumulation works.
Formatting note: keeping row_total as an integer matters because later you use '{:>3d}'.format(row_total) to print it; using 0 ensures the formatting call expects and receives an int.

Watch out for type errors: if `medal_counts[i][j]` is not an int (for example the country name or a string), the 'd' specifier will raise a TypeError. This is why the inner loop starts at 1 (to skip the country name in column 0).

distractors.description: You might choose this because it is a Pythonic way to loop over a list of rows and seems simpler. However, the rest of the code expects an index variable named i and uses expressions like medal_counts[i][0]. If you change the loop header to 'for row in medal_counts:' you introduce a different loop variable (row) but you do not update the later code. This mismatch causes a NameError (because i is not defined) or other errors if you tried to use the wrong variable. The core misconception is thinking direct element iteration can be dropped into code that uses numeric indices without changing the inner code. The program will fail unless you also rewrite the body to use row instead of indexing.

You might choose this because it only swaps the two indices and still looks like it reads a medal count. However, that swap changes which element you access. Here j acts as a row index and i as a column index. Since j ranges over medal columns (1..3) and i ranges over country rows (0..6), this can try to access elements that don't exist (for example, using i=4 as a column index on a row that has only 4 entries yields an IndexError). Even if sizes matched, you'd be summing the wrong entries (transposed values) so the totals would be incorrect or the program might crash. The distractor misaddresses which axis is the country and which is the medal column.

[backfilled] You might pick this because you see a 2D structure and assume the outer loop should use the length of an inner row. If you use this line, the loop runs for the number of columns (4) instead of the number of country-rows (7). As a result, the program will only process the first four country rows and skip the rest. The rest of the code still accesses medal_counts[i][...], so no immediate indexing error will appear for the smaller i range, but your output will omit countries. This distractor targets the common mix-up between row-count and column-count in a matrix. The mistake is that you are iterating over the wrong dimension: you are controlling how many rows to print by the number of columns, which leads to incomplete output rather than a crash.

That causes an IndexError and the program will crash. This distractor plays on the frequent off-by-one mistake: confusing inclusive/exclusive bounds and 0-based indexing in code. The problem is that you are shifting the index range incorrectly so the loop both omits data and eventually accesses an invalid index.
